entries.label: Exponents multiplied instead of added
entries.description: Multiplies the exponents when multiplying powers of the same base.
entries.signal: The exponent in the answer is the product of the two exponents.

refutation.text_md: You kept the base, which is right — the only question is what happens to the exponents.
Same base, multiply the powers: ADD the exponents, $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$.

entries.label: Bases multiplied as well
entries.description: Multiplies the bases together as well as combining the exponents.

refutation.text_md: Multiplying the numbers you see is a natural first move.
Here the base stays the base: $3^2 \times 3^4 = 3^6$, not $9^6$.

entries.label: Exponents added for a power of a power
entries.description: Adds the exponents when raising a power to a power.
entries.signal: The exponent in the answer is the sum of the two exponents.

refutation.text_md: Adding exponents is the rule you just learned for a product, so it is a reasonable thing to reach for.
$(x^3)^2$ is $x^3 \times x^3$: that is $x^{3+3} = x^6$, two lots of three.
A power of a power MULTIPLIES the exponents: $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$.
